sources.title: Neon: Logical replication in Neon
supports: Logical replication is enabled per project, sets wal_level to logical for good, and restarts all computes
Neon removes replication slots that have been inactive for about 40 hours, and a compute with a connected subscriber does not scale to zero
Roles created via SQL cannot be given the REPLICATION privilege; Neon supports the pgoutput and wal2json plugins

sources.title: Neon: Migrate data from Postgres with pg_dump and pg_restore
supports: pg_dump must use an unpooled connection string

sources.title: Neon: Migrate with AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)
supports: Neon documents AWS DMS with Neon as the target only

sources.title: What is Elastic Disaster Recovery?
supports: Source servers are replicated to a staging area subnet in your account, in the Region you select
Drill and recovery instances are launched from the most up-to-date state or a previous point in time
After recovery you can keep applications on AWS or replicate back to the primary site and fail back

sources.title: Elastic Disaster Recovery initialization and permissions
supports: The service must be initialized in each Region before use; the console does it when the default replication settings are saved
Initialization creates AWSServiceRoleForElasticDisasterRecovery and the Replication Server, Conversion Server, Recovery Instance, Agent, Failback, and RecoveryInstanceWithLaunchActions roles
Initialization through the API is `aws drs initialize-service`, after which the replication settings template still has to be created

sources.title: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery supported AWS Regions
supports: ap-northeast-1 (Tokyo) and ap-northeast-3 (Osaka) are supported

sources.title: Elastic Disaster Recovery network requirements
supports: Source servers talk to drs.<region>.amazonaws.com on TCP 443, continuously
Source servers send replicated data to the replication servers on TCP 1500
The staging area subnet needs the DRS endpoint on TCP 443, S3, and outbound access to the EC2 endpoint of its Region
The S3 buckets to allow include aws-elastic-disaster-recovery-<REGION> and the Amazon Linux 2023 repository bucket, because replication servers run Amazon Linux 2023
Replication uses TLS 1.2 from the agent to the replication server

sources.title: Elastic Disaster Recovery network setting preparations
supports: The staging area subnet is named in the replication template; a dedicated subnet is the stated best practice
Drill and recovery instances launch in the subnet named in each source server's EC2 launch template, which is created when the server is added

sources.title: Elastic Disaster Recovery network diagrams
supports: Supported sources are on premises, other clouds, and EC2 across Regions or across Availability Zones
Cross-Region replication is recommended over cross-AZ for protection against Region-level events

sources.title: Installing the agent on a secured network
supports: An interface VPC endpoint for DRS carries management traffic only; replication data goes directly from the source to the replication servers
A staging area in a private subnet also needs an EC2 interface endpoint and an S3 gateway endpoint
The installer takes --endpoint and --s3-endpoint for endpoint-specific DNS names
sources.note: The page describes an on-premises source reaching the endpoints over VPN or Direct Connect. That an agent inside the VPC finds the endpoint through private DNS without --endpoint follows from the VPC documentation, and was not tried.

sources.title: AWS services that integrate with AWS PrivateLink
supports: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery has the endpoint service name com.amazonaws.region.drs

sources.title: Point in time (PIT) policy
supports: Snapshots can be kept for 1 to 365 days
The policy has exactly three rules; MINUTE (every 10, kept 60) and HOUR (every 1, kept 24) are fixed, and only the DAY rule's retention is configurable

sources.title: Replication related FAQ
supports: The default snapshot retention is 7 days
A t3.small replication server is provisioned by default; the typical ratio of volumes to replication servers is 15:1
Replication is crash consistent
Replication servers are recycled approximately every 14 days
Snapshots no longer used, or past the retention, are deleted automatically

sources.title: Elastic Disaster Recovery concepts FAQ
supports: The guide states an RPO typically in the sub-second range and an RTO typically ranging between 5 and 20 minutes
RPO is measured to the latest crash-consistent point copied to the staging area; data still in memory on the source is not there
The RTO depends on the operating system's boot time
"Use most recent data" needs a connection to the source server and may time out when it is offline

sources.title: Amazon EBS volumes (replication settings)
supports: By default disks of 125 GiB or less use Magnetic HDD staging volumes; the volume type setting affects larger disks
Changing the encryption option after replication has started restarts replication from the beginning

sources.title: Data routing and throttling
supports: By default data goes to the replication servers' automatically assigned public IPv4 addresses
With the private IP option, replication uses an existing private connection such as VPC peering

sources.title: Elastic Disaster Recovery security groups
supports: The default DRS security group opens inbound TCP 1500 and is monitored and repaired by the service; using it is the recommended setting

sources.title: AWS DRS supported Linux operating systems
supports: Amazon Linux 2023 is supported up to kernel version 6.12
arm64 is supported only for Graviton-based EC2 source instances that recover to AWS

sources.title: Installing the AWS Replication Agent on Linux
supports: The installer is architecture-specific and is downloaded from aws-elastic-disaster-recovery-<REGION>; the arm64 one is under latest/linux_arm64/
The installer runs as root, creates the aws-replication user, and adds it to sudoers
The root disk is always replicated; whole disks are replicated, not partitions

sources.title: Generating the required AWS credentials
supports: Temporary credentials from STS are the recommended way to install the agent

sources.title: Using an instance profile for agent installation in AWS
supports: On an EC2 instance no credentials have to be generated: an instance profile whose role has AWSElasticDisasterRecoveryEc2InstancePolicy is enough

sources.title: AWSElasticDisasterRecoveryEc2InstancePolicy
supports: Version v5 has five statements: installation and registration actions on *, drs:TagResource on create for source servers and source networks, ten agent actions on source-server/*, and sts:AssumeRole on DRSCrossAccountAgentAuthorizedRole_*

sources.title: Adding instances from the Amazon EC2 Console
supports: The console installs the agent through Systems Manager on instances that have AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore and AWSElasticDisasterRecoveryEc2InstancePolicy
Volumes that are offline, unmounted, or unformatted are not replicated
The target Region may be the Region the instance is in

sources.title: Key considerations for EC2 launch templates
supports: Without a default VPC the subnet has to be set in the launch template, or the launch fails
For an arm64 source server the instance type has to be a Graviton type; the launch fails on a mismatch
The launch template is deleted when the source server is disconnected

sources.title: Preparing for recovery
supports: A recovery drill is a non-disruptive test that performs the same steps as a recovery, with the same launch settings and snapshots
Drills are recommended at least quarterly
A drill can be performed once the initial sync has completed, even in lag or stall status
`aws drs start-recovery --source-servers ... --is-drill` starts a drill; `aws drs terminate-recovery-instances` cleans up
Drill instances are billed until deleted, and are cleaned up when the same server is drilled again

sources.title: Using Elastic Disaster Recovery for recovery and failback
supports: Recovery launches instances; failover, the redirection of traffic, is performed by you outside the service
For an EC2 source in the same account, failback is reversed replication started on the recovery instance

sources.title: Performing a failover with Elastic Disaster Recovery
supports: After the recovery instances are launched, you redirect traffic to them yourself
Launching a new recovery instance from the same source server cleans up the previous recovery instances

sources.title: Cross Availability Zone recovery
supports: Replication settings and the launch template name a subnet in an Availability Zone other than the instance's
Protecting the recovered instance starts replication from it back to the original zone, as a rescan and not a full sync, and stops replication of the original instance

sources.title: Performing a cross-Region failback
supports: Reversed replication copies the recovery instance's data back and creates a source server in the original Region
Stopping replication of the original source deletes all its points in time
Traffic redirection is not done by DRS; the guide suggests Amazon Route 53
Cross-Region replication, failover, and failback add data transfer and replication resource costs not in the pricing examples

sources.title: Performing a failback with Elastic Disaster Recovery
supports: Data written to the failover systems has to be replicated back before traffic is redirected
arm64 servers support failback within AWS only

sources.title: Launch into source instance
supports: The instance to launch into needs the tag AWSDRS=AllowLaunchingIntoThisInstance and the same architecture

sources.title: Source servers page command menus
supports: Disconnect from AWS uninstalls the agent and stops replication; only disconnected servers can be deleted
Stop replication ends the charges for replication and the staging area, and deletes all saved snapshots

sources.title: Best practices
supports: Source servers are billed by DRS and consume replication resources until Disconnect from AWS is performed
Disconnecting discards the points in time of the source server

sources.title: Source networks
supports: Network replication copies the configuration of an in-AWS VPC and recovers it as a CloudFormation stack

sources.title: Configuring the default post-launch actions
supports: Post-launch actions are SSM command or automation documents run after a launch; predefined ones verify HTTP responses, connectivity, disk space, and tags

sources.title: Orchestrating recovery with recovery plans
supports: A recovery plan launches groups of source servers in ordered steps, with optional waits, as a drill or as a recovery

sources.title: Alarm events and EventBridge
supports: Events have source aws.drs and the detail types DRS Source Server Launch Result, DRS Source Server Data Replication Stalled Change, DRS Recovery Instance Failback State Change, and DRS PIT Snapshot Taken
The launch result carries state, job-id, and is-drill as the strings TRUE or FALSE

sources.title: CloudWatch Metrics for DRS
supports: DRS publishes LagDuration (the age of the latest consistent snapshot, in seconds), Backlog (bytes yet to be synced), and DurationSinceLastSuccessfulRecoveryLaunch

sources.title: Recovery dashboard
supports: When replication is stalled, the dashboard shows the replication initiation steps and where the error occurred
Lag is how far behind the source a recovery instance launched now would be

sources.title: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery endpoints and quotas
supports: 300 replicating source servers per account and Region, not adjustable; 20 concurrent jobs; one job per source server at a time; one launch configuration template per account and Region

sources.title: StartRecovery
supports: isDrill is a boolean; each source server may name a recoverySnapshotID or get an on-demand snapshot

sources.title: DisconnectSourceServer
supports: Replication stops immediately and the replication resources are deleted within 90 minutes
A source server that has a recovery instance cannot be disconnected

sources.title: DataReplicationInfo
supports: lagDuration is a string of 1 to 64 characters with no stated format
dataReplicationState is one of STOPPED, INITIATING, INITIAL_SYNC, BACKLOG, CREATING_SNAPSHOT, CONTINUOUS, PAUSED, RESCAN, STALLED, DISCONNECTED

sources.title: @aws-sdk/client-drs 3.1149.0
supports: Member names and enum values of SourceServer, RecoverySnapshot, Job, RecoveryInstance, and the requests of StartRecovery, TerminateRecoveryInstances, CreateReplicationConfigurationTemplate, and CreateLaunchConfigurationTemplate
sources.note: Read from the type definitions in the npm tarball.

sources.title: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery pricing
supports: A flat hourly fee per replicating source server, whatever the number of disks, drills, or the Region
Staging disks, snapshots, replication servers, and launched instances are billed by EBS and EC2 on top
One base snapshot per source disk, the size of that disk, plus incremental snapshots for the retention
A conversion server runs for several minutes per launch and generally costs less than USD 0.05

sources.title: AWS Price List: Elastic Disaster Recovery, ap-northeast-1
supports: APN1-DRS-Replication: USD 0.028 per replication hour

sources.title: AWS Price List: Amazon EC2, ap-northeast-1 (CSV)
supports: APN1-BoxUsage:t3.small, Linux, shared tenancy: USD 0.0272 per hour
APN1-EBS:VolumeUsage (Magnetic): USD 0.08 per GB-month; APN1-EBS:VolumeIOUsage: USD 0.08 per million I/O requests
sources.note: The same offer file as the JSON the other chapters cite, publication 2026-10-09T20:31:34Z, read as CSV and filtered by usage type.

sources.title: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery FAQs
supports: Backup and disaster recovery are described as complementary; backups are used for long-term retention

sources.title: AWS Backup: backup plan options and configuration
supports: Snapshot backups can be retained from 1 day to 100 years, or indefinitely

sources.title: CloudFormation resource provider schemas
supports: CloudFormation publishes one zip of resource provider schemas per Region, and says to check a resource's availability in a Region against that Region's schemas
sources.note: On 2026-10-13 the zips for us-east-1 and us-west-2 contained aws-drs-launchconfigurationtemplate, aws-drs-recoveryplan, aws-drs-replicationconfigurationtemplate, and aws-drs-sourcenetwork. The zips for ap-northeast-1, ap-northeast-3, us-east-2, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1 contained no aws-drs file. The Template Reference's table of contents had no AWS::DRS section.

sources.title: aws-cdk-lib 2.273.0: aws-drs
supports: The module has three L1 constructs: CfnReplicationConfigurationTemplate, CfnLaunchConfigurationTemplate, and CfnSourceNetwork
sources.note: Read from the type definitions in the installed package.

sources.title: cdkd 0.296.28: provider registry
supports: Dedicated providers exist for AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup, AWS::Events::Rule, AWS::IAM::ManagedPolicy, AWS::IAM::Policy, AWS::IAM::Role, AWS::Lambda::Function, AWS::Lambda::Permission, and AWS::Logs::LogGroup
There is none for AWS::EC2::VPCEndpoint, AWS::EC2::SecurityGroupEgress, or any AWS::DRS type, which therefore go through Cloud Control API
sources.note: Read from the bundled JavaScript of the installed package.

sources.title: How Workers works
supports: Workers run on Cloudflare's global network, on isolates rather than a virtual machine per function, and a request is handled by the data center that receives it

sources.title: Configuring regions for Vercel Functions
supports: Vercel Functions run in the regions set for the project, with multiple availability zone redundancy by default
Enterprise teams can set functionFailoverRegions for the Node.js runtime

sources.title: Architect for AWS Fargate for Amazon ECS
supports: Each Fargate task has its own isolation boundary and does not share the underlying kernel, CPU resources, memory resources, or elastic network interface with another task

sources.title: Linux containers on Fargate container image pull behavior for Amazon ECS
supports: Every Fargate task runs on its own single use, single tenant instance
Images and layers are not cached: the whole image is pulled for every task, and the pull time is directly correlated to the time taken to start a task
The size of the image, the compression algorithm, and the number of vCPUs affect the time; zstd decompresses faster
For images larger than 250 MB lazy loading may be better than downloading all of the image

sources.title: Fargate platform versions for Amazon ECS
supports: The LATEST Linux platform version is 1.4.0
Each task runs on one platform version revision during its lifecycle; to use the latest revision you must start a new task
A service changes platform version through a new deployment; tasks added by scaling get the version of the service's current deployment

sources.title: Fargate Linux platform version change log
supports: 1.4.0 is the only Linux platform version listed as available; it is based on Amazon Linux 2
sources.note: The deprecation table on platform-versions-retired.html gives June 15, 2026 for 1.3.0.

sources.title: Task retirement and maintenance for AWS Fargate on Amazon ECS
supports: When a platform version revision is retired, all tasks running on it are stopped; running tasks are never migrated
Notices go to the AWS Health Dashboard and by email; the default wait before retirement is 7 days
Service tasks are replaced by the scheduler: with the defaults (minimum healthy percent 100, maximum percent 200) a new task is started and running before an old one is retired
A standalone task is stopped on or after the retirement date and is not replaced
If a replacement cannot be launched, the retired task is stopped without one
A fault in the underlying host is handled by replacing the host without a retirement notice
Task retirement cannot be opted out of
sources.note: The page credits maximumPercent in one passage and minimum healthy percent in another for start-before-stop.

sources.title: Prepare for AWS Fargate task retirement on Amazon ECS
supports: The account setting fargateTaskRetirementWaitPeriod takes 0, 7 (the default), or 14 days
Since 2025-12-18 an EC2 event window can be configured for Fargate tasks (fargateEventWindows) and takes precedence over the wait period

sources.title: Amazon ECS task definition differences for Fargate
supports: The task size table: 256 CPU units with 512 MiB, 1 GB, 2 GB; 512 with 1 to 4 GB; 1024 with 2 to 8 GB; 2048 with 4 to 16 GB in 1 GB steps; 4096 with 8 to 30 GB in 1 GB steps; 8192 with 16 to 60 GB in 4 GB steps; 16384 with 32 to 120 GB in 8 GB steps; 32768 with 60, 120, or 244 GB
The 8, 16, and 32 vCPU sizes need Linux platform version 1.4.0 or later
Tasks on Linux platform version 1.4.0 can use Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexes to start without waiting for the whole image; new users are limited to index manifest v2
SOCI works for X86_64 and ARM64, for images in Amazon ECR private registries, compressed with gzip or not at all (not zstd), and is recommended for images larger than 250 MiB compressed

sources.title: Fargate task ephemeral storage for Amazon ECS
supports: Tasks on platform version 1.4.0 or later receive a minimum of 20 GiB of ephemeral storage, which can be increased to a maximum of 200 GiB with the ephemeralStorage parameter
The pulled, compressed, and uncompressed image is stored on the ephemeral storage
sources.note: What happens when the storage fills was not found on the pages read.

sources.title: Amazon ECS API Reference: EphemeralStorage
supports: sizeInGiB: the minimum supported value is 21 GiB and the maximum is 200 GiB

sources.title: Amazon ECS task definition parameters for Fargate
supports: Task-level memory is the hard limit of memory to present to the task
If a container attempts to exceed its container-level memory, the container is killed

sources.title: Troubleshooting Amazon ECS OutOfMemoryError errors
supports: The error 'container killed due to memory usage' occurs when a container exits because its processes consumed more memory than was allocated in the task definition
sources.note: The exact stoppedReason text and an exit code for Fargate were not found on the pages read.

sources.title: Amazon ECS CloudWatch metrics
supports: For Fargate, CPUUtilization and MemoryUtilization in the AWS/ECS namespace exist per service: usage divided by what the service's tasks reserve
The metrics are sent in 1-minute periods without any setup
sources.note: The 1-minute period and the automatic metrics are stated on cloudwatch-metrics.html.

sources.title: Amazon ECS Container Insights metrics
supports: Container Insights adds CpuUtilized, CpuReserved, MemoryUtilized, MemoryReserved, EphemeralStorageUtilized and others in the ECS/ContainerInsights namespace, by cluster, service, and task definition family
CpuUtilized is in CPU units; MemoryUtilized is in MiB although the unit is labelled megabytes

sources.title: Amazon ECS Container Insights with enhanced observability metrics
supports: Enhanced observability adds task-level and container-level metrics such as TaskCpuUtilization, TaskMemoryUtilization, ContainerCpuUtilized, and ContainerMemoryUtilized

sources.title: Monitor Amazon ECS containers using Container Insights with enhanced observability
supports: Metrics collected by Container Insights are charged as custom metrics
The cluster setting containerInsights takes enabled or enhanced; the account default is disabled
sources.note: The setting's values and the account default are on ecs-account-settings.html.

sources.title: Amazon CloudWatch Pricing
supports: Container Insights with enhanced observability for ECS is priced per metric, per month, prorated by the hour
Pricing example 19 counts, for Fargate without enhanced observability, 13 metrics per cluster, 15 per service (RunningTaskCount at no charge from 2026-10-01), and 10 per task, aggregated by name
sources.note: The page's numbers are for US East (N. Virginia).

sources.title: Amazon ECS endpoints and quotas
supports: Fargate On-Demand vCPU resource count: 6 by default in each supported Region, adjustable
Fargate Spot vCPU resource count: 6 by default in each supported Region, adjustable
Fargate On-Demand and Spot launch rates outside the 16 listed Regions: burst 100, sustained 20 per second, adjustable
Rate of tasks launched by a service on Fargate: 500 per minute outside the listed Regions, not adjustable
Tasks launched per run-task: 10
New accounts might start with lower quotas, which Fargate raises automatically with usage
sources.note: ap-northeast-1 is not among the 16 Regions with the lower launch rates.

sources.title: AWS Fargate throttling quotas
supports: Fargate limits task launch rates with a token bucket per account and Region: 100 tokens, refilled at 20 a second
Launch rates in practice also depend on the image to download and unpack, health checks, and load balancer registration
The rate quota for RunTask is 20 calls per second, each launching up to 10 tasks

sources.title: AWS Fargate Pricing
supports: Fargate is billed for requested vCPU, memory, operating system, CPU architecture, and storage from the start of the image download until the task terminates, per second with a 1-minute minimum
20 GB of ephemeral storage is included; only additional storage is billed, per GB-hour
Fargate Spot runs interrupt-tolerant tasks at up to a 70% discount; its prices are set by AWS Fargate and adjust gradually
Fargate Spot is available for Linux on x86 and ARM
Savings Plans offer up to 50% on Fargate for a commitment in dollars per hour over one or three years
sources.note: The price tables are filled in by script; no Tokyo number, on demand or Spot, is in the page's static text.

sources.title: AWS Price List: Amazon ECS, ap-northeast-1
supports: Fargate ephemeral storage: USD 0.000133 per GB-hour
Fargate ARM: USD 0.04045 per vCPU-hour and USD 0.00442 per GB-hour; x86: USD 0.05056 and USD 0.00553
The offer has no Fargate Spot price
sources.note: Offer published 2026-09-11T12:44:25Z.

sources.title: AWS Price List: Amazon CloudWatch, ap-northeast-1
supports: APN1-CW:MetricsUsage: USD 0.07 per metric-month, the Container Insights with enhanced observability rate
sources.note: Offer published 2026-10-07T11:55:40Z. That this usage type is the one billed for ECS enhanced observability was inferred from the pricing page's USD 0.07 example.

sources.title: Amazon ECS clusters for Fargate
supports: A capacity provider must be associated with a cluster before a strategy can name it; a strategy has at most 20 providers
Only one provider in a strategy can have a base; at least one needs a weight above zero
A service can be changed from a launch type to a capacity provider strategy, with a forced new deployment
A Fargate Spot task gets a two-minute warning before it is stopped, as a task state change event and as SIGTERM to the task
When Spot capacity is unavailable, services retry until it is; Fargate does not replace Spot capacity with on-demand capacity
The stop code of an interrupted task is SpotInterruption; stopTimeout can be at most 120 seconds

sources.title: Amazon ECS API Reference: CapacityProviderStrategyItem
supports: base is how many tasks, at a minimum, run on the provider; it is satisfied before weights; range 0 to 100,000
weight is the relative share of tasks beyond the base; range 0 to 1,000; weights 1 and 4 mean one task on A for every four on B
FARGATE_SPOT supports Linux X86_64 on platform version 1.3.0 or later and ARM64 on 1.4.0 or later

sources.title: Use a target metric to scale Amazon ECS services
supports: The service scales out proportionally to the metric as fast as it can, and scales in more gradually
With several target tracking policies it scales out if any is ready and in only if all are
A policy does not scale on insufficient data
ALBRequestCountPerTarget is not supported for the blue/green deployment type
Scale-in is turned off while a deployment is in progress

sources.title: Automatically scale your Amazon ECS service
supports: Target tracking, step scaling, scheduled scaling, and predictive scaling are supported
Scale-in is blocked until the scale-in cooldown has expired; a scale-out during it happens immediately
Scaling starts from the running task count, not the desired count
With a minimum capacity of 0 and target tracking, Service Auto Scaling waits for one data point of demand and then scales out by the minimum possible amount
Step scaling lets you react more quickly because you define the thresholds and adjustments yourself

sources.title: How target tracking scaling for Application Auto Scaling works
supports: The default cooldown for ECS services is 300 seconds
Scale-in happens only when utilization is far enough below the target, usually more than 10% lower
A metric that emits real zeros, such as ALBRequestCountPerTarget, lets a target with minimum capacity 0 scale in to 0
A scheduled action can start a scaling activity during a cooldown

sources.title: Application Auto Scaling API Reference: PredefinedMetricSpecification
supports: ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization, ECSServiceAverageMemoryUtilization, and ALBRequestCountPerTarget are predefined metric types; high-resolution variants of the first two use 20-second metrics
ResourceLabel is app/<load-balancer-name>/<load-balancer-id>/targetgroup/<target-group-name>/<target-group-id>
sources.note: DisableScaleIn and the cooldown fields are on API_TargetTrackingScalingPolicyConfiguration.html.

sources.title: Use scheduled actions to scale Amazon ECS services
supports: Scheduled actions change the number of tasks at set times; scaling policies keep working inside the minimum and maximum the action set

sources.title: Optimizing Amazon ECS service auto scaling
supports: A scaling metric has to be correlated with demand and change in proportion to capacity; load testing is how to find it
Scaling on memory is not recommended for garbage-collected runtimes, whose memory use is often uncorrelated with throughput

sources.title: Protect your Amazon ECS tasks from being terminated by scale-in events
supports: Task scale-in protection keeps a service's task from being terminated by scale-in from service auto scaling or deployments: 2 hours by default, 48 hours at most
A container sets it at $ECS_AGENT_URI/task-protection/v1/state; the task role needs ecs:GetTaskProtection and ecs:UpdateTaskProtection
It is supported only for tasks deployed from a service

sources.title: Monitor Amazon ECS containers with ECS Exec
supports: ECS Exec uses Systems Manager Session Manager; the agent's binaries are bind-mounted into the container
Commands run as root, even when the container specifies a user
A read-only root file system (readonlyRootFilesystem) is not supported, because the agent has to write to the container's file system
ECS Exec cannot be turned on for existing tasks, only for new ones
A session's idle timeout is 20 minutes and cannot be changed
CloudTrail records an ExecuteCommand event; commands and output can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3
Access can be limited with condition keys such as ecs:container-name and ecs:ResourceTag, and enabling it can be denied with ecs:enable-execute-command
Tasks without internet access need the ssmmessages interface endpoint
initProcessEnabled is recommended to clean up zombie processes

sources.title: Amazon ECS task IAM role: ECS Exec permissions
supports: ECS Exec needs ssmmessages:CreateControlChannel, CreateDataChannel, OpenControlChannel, and OpenDataChannel on the task role, with Resource *

sources.title: Install the Session Manager plugin for the AWS CLI
supports: Starting Session Manager sessions with the AWS CLI requires the Session Manager plugin on the local machine
sources.note: The ECS Exec page read on the same day does not mention the plugin.

sources.title: Amazon ECS interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink)
supports: Tasks using Fargate do not require the interface endpoints for Amazon ECS itself, but may need the ones for Amazon ECR, Secrets Manager, or CloudWatch Logs

sources.title: Amazon ECR interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink)
supports: Fargate tasks on platform version 1.4.0 or later need both ECR endpoints (ecr.dkr and ecr.api) and the S3 gateway endpoint
With the awslogs driver and no internet gateway, the com.amazonaws.region.logs interface endpoint is required

sources.title: Using Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to schedule Amazon ECS tasks
supports: EventBridge Scheduler runs ECS tasks on rate, cron, and one-time schedules, in any time zone
To use a capacity provider strategy, a capacity provider must be associated with the cluster
A retry policy re-runs the schedule if it fails to invoke its target

sources.title: EventBridge Scheduler API Reference: EcsParameters
supports: EcsParameters is the templated target for ECS RunTask: TaskDefinitionArn is required; CapacityProviderStrategy, LaunchType, NetworkConfiguration, PlatformVersion, and EnableExecuteCommand are optional
sources.note: What the Target's Input means for an ECS templated target was not found on the pages read.

sources.title: Amazon ECS API Reference: RunTask
supports: count: up to 10 tasks for each call
clientToken ensures the idempotency of the request; reusing it with different parameters is a ConflictException
overrides.containerOverrides can replace the command, environment variables, cpu, and memory of a named container for one run
sources.note: The override fields are on API_ContainerOverride.html and API_TaskOverride.html.

sources.title: Amazon ECS standalone tasks
supports: A standalone task is for an application that performs some work and then stops, such as a batch process

sources.title: Amazon ECS task state change events
supports: For a stopped task the event's stoppedReason and stopCode say why it stopped

sources.title: AWS::ECS::Service
supports: If a capacityProviderStrategy is specified, the launchType parameter must be omitted
EnableExecuteCommand is a property of the service

sources.title: Pass Secrets Manager secrets through Amazon ECS environment variables
supports: A secret is injected when the container is initially started; after a rotation the container does not get the new value until a new task is launched
valueFrom may name a JSON key and a version: arn:...:secret:secret-name:json-key:version-stage:version-id (platform version 1.4.0 or later)
sources.note: The task execution role needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue (task_execution_IAM_role.html). Parameter Store: secrets-envvar-ssm-paramstore.html.

sources.title: Amazon ECS API Reference: HealthCheck
supports: Container health check defaults: interval 30 seconds, timeout 5 seconds, retries 3, start period off
A service task that reports unhealthy is stopped and replaced; a task run manually continues regardless of its health status

sources.title: Amazon ECS API Reference: LogConfiguration
supports: On June 25, 2025 the default log driver mode changed from blocking to non-blocking; the account setting defaultLogDriverMode changes it back
In blocking mode a write to stdout blocks when logs cannot be sent; in non-blocking mode logs go to a buffer of max-buffer-size and can be lost

sources.title: Send Amazon ECS logs to an AWS service or AWS Partner
supports: FireLens routes logs to AWS services or partner destinations with Fluentd or Fluent Bit, as a container in the task

sources.title: What are Savings Plans?
supports: Savings Plans trade a commitment to an amount of compute, measured per hour, for one or three years against lower prices
Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2 regardless of family, size, or Region, and also to Fargate and Lambda
sources.note: Whether Fargate Spot usage counts was not found.

sources.title: Cloudflare Containers: Limits and Instance Types
supports: Six predefined instance types from lite (1/16 vCPU, 256 MiB, 2 GB disk) to standard-4 (4 vCPU, 12 GiB, 20 GB disk); custom types up to 4 vCPU and 12 GiB
Account defaults: 6 TiB of memory, 1,500 vCPU, and 30 TB of disk concurrently

sources.title: Cloudflare Containers: Scaling and Routing
supports: Requests are spread over a fixed number of instances with the getRandom helper; built-in autoscaling and routing are planned
sources.note: The FAQ (developers.cloudflare.com/containers/faq/) says built-in autoscaling for stateless applications is not available today, cold starts are often 1 to 3 seconds, and sleepAfter is 10 minutes by default.

sources.title: Cloudflare Containers: Cron container
supports: A Workers Cron Trigger starts a container that does a short task and exits

sources.title: Vercel Knowledge Base: Does Vercel support Docker deployments?
supports: Vercel runs OCI-compatible container images as Vercel Functions: it builds the image from a Dockerfile.vercel, stores it in Vercel Container Registry, and serves it from a function that scales automatically

sources.title: Vercel Functions Limits
supports: With Fluid compute the maximum duration is 300 seconds on Hobby and 800 seconds on Pro and Enterprise, with an extended 1,800 seconds in beta

sources.title: Vercel Cron Jobs
supports: A cron job is an HTTP GET request to a path of the project's production deployment

sources.title: cdkd v0.296.28: providers for ECS, Scheduler, and Application Auto Scaling
supports: AWS::ECS::Cluster, TaskDefinition, and Service share one provider, which handles CapacityProviders on the cluster and CapacityProviderStrategy and EnableExecuteCommand on the service
AWS::Scheduler::Schedule has a provider that handles Target, including EcsParameters, and ScheduleExpressionTimezone

No provider is registered for AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget, ScalingPolicy, AWS::EC2::SecurityGroupEgress, or AWS::ECS::ClusterCapacityProviderAssociations, and none is on the unsupported list, so they go through Cloud Control API
sources.note: Read from the v0.296.28 tag: register-providers.ts, providers/ecs-provider.ts, providers/scheduler-schedule-provider.ts, unsupported-types.generated.ts.

sources.title: aws-cdk-lib 2.273.0: what the ECS constructs synthesize
supports: enableFargateCapacityProviders creates an AWS::ECS::ClusterCapacityProviderAssociations resource that the service does not depend on
FargateService with enableExecuteCommand adds the four ssmmessages actions and logs actions on Resource * to the task role
FargateTaskDefinition.grantRun grants ecs:RunTask on the task definition and iam:PassRole on its two roles, conditioned on ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com
sources.note: Observed by synthesizing with the pinned version on 2026-10-13, not read from documentation.

sources.title: AWS Firewall Manager
supports: Firewall Manager applies protections across the accounts and resources of an organization, including accounts and resources added later
Charges incurred by Firewall Manager are for the underlying services, such as AWS WAF and AWS Config

sources.title: AWS Firewall Manager prerequisites
supports: The prerequisite steps, in order: AWS Organizations, a default administrator account, AWS Config, the Marketplace subscription for third-party policies, AWS RAM sharing for Network Firewall and DNS Firewall policies, and Regions that are disabled by default

sources.title: Joining and configuring AWS Organizations for using Firewall Manager
supports: The account must be a member of an organization in AWS Organizations
The organization must have all features enabled; consolidated billing alone is not enough

sources.title: Creating an AWS Firewall Manager default administrator account
supports: Only the organization's management account can create the default administrator account
The default administrator has full administrative scope and is set as an AWS Organizations delegated administrator for Firewall Manager

sources.title: Enabling AWS Config for using Firewall Manager
supports: AWS Config must be enabled for each member account, including the Firewall Manager administrator account, and for each Region that contains resources to protect
The recording frequency must be Continuous
The resource types AWS Config has to record for each policy type, when not recording all resources
AWS Config can record CloudFront distributions only in US East (N. Virginia)
A custom IAM role for the recorder that lacks permissions is not visible to Firewall Manager

sources.title: Enabling resource sharing for Network Firewall and DNS Firewall policies with AWS RAM
supports: Network Firewall and DNS Firewall policies need sharing with AWS Organizations enabled in AWS RAM

sources.title: Using AWS Firewall Manager administrators
supports: An organization can have several Firewall Manager administrators, each with an administrative scope of accounts or OUs, Regions, and policy types
The default administrator can manage third-party firewalls and has full scope, and is otherwise a peer of the other administrators

sources.title: Creating a Firewall Manager administrator account
supports: Only the management account can create Firewall Manager administrator accounts
An OU in a scope includes the accounts of its child OUs, including ones added later

sources.title: Changing the default Firewall Manager administrator account
supports: When an administrator revokes their account, all Firewall Manager policies created by that account are deleted

sources.title: Disqualifying changes to a Firewall Manager administrator account
supports: Closing the administrator account deactivates its policies and stops their protections; policy data is kept for 90 days

sources.title: Using AWS Firewall Manager policies
supports: The policy types: AWS WAF (and AWS WAF Classic), Shield Advanced, Amazon VPC security group, Amazon VPC network ACL, Network Firewall, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, and third-party firewall (Palo Alto Networks Cloud NGFW, Fortigate CNF)
A policy is specific to one policy type, and several policies of one type can exist
A policy either reports non-compliant accounts and resources or remediates them automatically

sources.title: Creating an AWS Firewall Manager policy
supports: An AWS WAF policy for CloudFront distributions is created with the Region set to Global; other Regions need one policy each
With automatic remediation, a policy can also remove existing web ACL associations that are not managed by another active Firewall Manager policy, associating its own web ACL first
A content audit security group policy must be created without automatic remediation
Resource tags can include or exclude, not both in one policy
The creation of a policy can take several minutes

sources.title: Using the AWS Firewall Manager policy scope
supports: Scope by accounts: all, an include list of accounts and OUs, or an exclude list
Scope by resource tags: all of the tags or any of the tags, included or excluded; a tag matches on the same key and the same value
A resource that leaves the scope stays associated and protected unless the policy removes protections from resources that leave the scope
The AWS Config managed rules and web ACLs with no resources are deleted regardless of that option

sources.title: Deleting an AWS Firewall Manager policy
supports: Deleting a Shield Advanced policy leaves the accounts subscribed to Shield Advanced
Replica security groups of a common security group policy remain unless the cleanup option is chosen

sources.title: Using AWS WAF policies with Firewall Manager
supports: A policy either creates new web ACLs for all in-scope resources, replacing ones in use, or retrofits the web ACLs already associated
In a managed web ACL an account can manage its own rules and rule groups in addition to the policy's

sources.title: Rule group management for AWS WAF policies
supports: A managed web ACL has three sets: the policy's first rule groups, the account's rules and rule groups, and the policy's last rule groups
The first and last sets take rule groups only, not individual rules
The rule groups are named PREFMManaged- and POSTFMManaged- followed by the policy name and a timestamp

sources.title: Web ACL management for AWS WAF policies
supports: With optimizeUnassociatedWebACL, a web ACL is created in an account only if a resource will use it; without it, every in-scope account gets one
A web ACL the policy creates is named FMManagedWebACLV2-<policy name>-<timestamp>
Retrofitting (webACLSource RETROFIT_EXISTING) requires the web ACL to be owned by the account and associated only with in-scope resources
A customer-owned web ACL that a customer associates manually is still overridden by the policy's web ACL

sources.title: Logging for an AWS WAF policy
supports: A logging change made through AWS WAF on a managed web ACL is not detected automatically; re-evaluating the policy's AWS Config rule prompts an update

sources.title: Setting up AWS Firewall Manager AWS WAF policies
supports: Web ACLs that Firewall Manager creates cannot take part in CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans
After deleting a policy with its resources, the changes might take a few minutes to reach all accounts

sources.title: Using security group policies in Firewall Manager to manage Amazon VPC security groups
supports: Best practices: exclude the administrator account, start with automatic remediation disabled, and keep Firewall Manager and other tools from managing the same security groups
Changes to security groups on EC2 network interfaces are usually detected within several hours, and can take as much as six
Network interfaces created by Amazon RDS are not supported, and those of Fargate tasks and requester-managed interfaces cannot be updated

sources.title: Using content audit security group policies with Firewall Manager
supports: A content audit policy applies to customer-created security groups in scope, for the resource types EC2 instance, network interface, and security group
The audit security group is created in the administrator account and is only a comparison reference
With custom policy rules, allow means every in-scope rule must be within the allowed range of the audit group's rules; deny means none may be
With automatic remediation, Firewall Manager updates or removes non-compliant rules
Peer security groups cannot be referenced in a content audit policy

sources.title: Using common security group policies with Firewall Manager
supports: A common security group policy replicates primary security groups from the administrator account into the VPCs in scope and associates them

sources.title: Using usage audit security group policies with Firewall Manager
supports: A usage audit policy reports unused and redundant security groups and, with remediation, removes or consolidates them

sources.title: Using AWS Shield Advanced policies in Firewall Manager
supports: A Shield Advanced policy applies Shield Advanced protection to the chosen resource types

sources.title: Using Amazon VPC network ACL policies with Firewall Manager
supports: A network ACL policy enforces first and last rules in the network ACLs of in-scope subnets; accounts add rules in between

sources.title: Using AWS Network Firewall policies in Firewall Manager
supports: A Network Firewall policy creates and manages firewalls for the VPCs in scope, distributed, centralized, or imported

sources.title: Using Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall policies in Firewall Manager
supports: A DNS Firewall policy associates rule groups with the VPCs in scope, before and after the account's own associations

sources.title: Viewing compliance information for an AWS Firewall Manager policy
supports: Compliance is shown per account and per resource; a content audit policy has violation details for a security group rule, the referenced audit rule, the reason, and a suggested remediation
After a change to the policy or to in-scope resources, the compliance status may take several minutes to update
Firewall Manager detects changes through AWS Config, and rapid repeated changes can lose compliance or remediation state

supports: Firewall Manager sends findings for non-compliant resources to Security Hub CSPM automatically when Security Hub is in use
The product name to filter on is Firewall Manager, case sensitive
Findings are not resolved for deleted policies, deleted resources, or resources that have left the scope

sources.title: What is AWS Glue?
supports: AWS Glue is a serverless data integration service; its features are grouped as discovering and organizing data (the Data Catalog, crawlers), transforming data (jobs), and building and monitoring pipelines (triggers, workflows)
Related services named on the page: AWS Lake Formation as an authorization layer over the Data Catalog, and AWS Glue DataBrew

sources.title: AWS Glue for Ray end of support
supports: AWS Glue for Ray is closed to new customers starting April 30, 2026; existing customers can continue; no new features are planned
The alternative AWS recommends is Ray on Amazon EKS with the KubeRay operator

sources.title: Configuring job properties for Spark jobs in AWS Glue
supports: Job types and their commands: Spark (glueetl), Spark Streaming (gluestreaming), Python shell (pythonshell)
AWS Glue versions: 6.0 is Spark 4.1.1 and Python 3.13, 5.1 is Spark 3.5.6 and Python 3.11; a job created without a version gets 5.1
A DPU is 4 vCPUs and 16 GB of memory; G.1X is 1 DPU per worker, G.2X is 2 DPU; G.025X is for streaming jobs only
The job timeout defaults to 480 minutes for AWS Glue 5.0 and later (2,880 for 4.0 and earlier); the maximum is 10,080 minutes; jobs are billed for execution time
Number of retries is 0 to 10; a job that reaches its timeout is not restarted
Maximum concurrency defaults to 1 and an error is returned when it is reached
The flexible execution class is for non-urgent jobs, and is supported with G.1X and G.2X on AWS Glue 3.0 or later
Jobs that access Lake Formation tables with cell-level filters cannot use job bookmarks or push-down predicates

sources.title: AWS Glue versions
supports: AWS Glue 5.1 is the default version for jobs created without specifying one
AWS Glue 6.0 removes EMRFS and uses S3A as the only S3 connector

sources.title: Configuring job properties for Python shell jobs in AWS Glue
supports: Python shell jobs run Python 3.9; Python shell 3.6 reached end of life on June 1, 2026
Job bookmarks cannot be used with Python shell jobs

sources.title: Migrate from AWS Glue Python shell jobs
supports: AWS documents alternatives to Python shell jobs: AWS Glue Spark jobs, AWS Lambda, and Amazon ECS on Fargate
The minimum number of workers of an AWS Glue Spark job is 2
AWS Lambda's maximum timeout is 900 seconds

sources.title: Tracking processed data using job bookmarks
supports: A job bookmark is state persisted from a job run so that later runs process only new data; the default option is Disable, with which the job always processes the entire dataset
For Amazon S3 sources the bookmark checks the last modified time of objects; a timestamp is used to filter the new files
The state elements are saved atomically when job.commit is invoked from the user script
Only source files are tracked: when a bookmark is rewound or reset, AWS Glue does not clean the target files, and the page suggests different output targets to avoid duplicate data
Bookmarks are kept per job and are deleted with the job
Changing a source's path without changing its transformation_ctx makes the job use the old bookmark state and skip files

sources.title: Using job bookmarks
supports: Bookmarks do not work without job.init at the beginning of the script and job.commit at the end
A dynamic frame method called without transformation_ctx does not take part in the bookmark

sources.title: Using job parameters in AWS Glue jobs
supports: --job-bookmark-option takes job-bookmark-enable, job-bookmark-disable or job-bookmark-pause
Arguments set on a job run override the job's DefaultArguments, and NonOverridableArguments override both
Job arguments are limited to 260 KB

sources.title: Accessing parameters using getResolvedOptions
supports: getResolvedOptions(sys.argv, [names]) returns the named arguments; names are passed with two leading hyphens and may contain underscores, not hyphens

sources.title: Logging for AWS Glue jobs
supports: In AWS Glue 5.0 all jobs log in real time: system, Spark daemon and AWS Glue logger output to /aws-glue/jobs/error, user stdout and stderr to /aws-glue/jobs/output
--custom-logGroup-prefix replaces the prefix, giving <prefix>/error and <prefix>/output

sources.title: Step 2: Create an IAM role for AWS Glue
supports: Data sources require s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject; data targets require s3:ListBucket, s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject
The console's default is the managed policy AWSGlueServiceRole; the page also allows a policy of your own for specific Amazon S3 resources

sources.title: AWSGlueServiceRole (AWS managed policy reference)
supports: The managed policy allows glue:*, cloudwatch:PutMetricData, Amazon S3 actions on buckets named aws-glue-*, and logs:CreateLogGroup, CreateLogStream and PutLogEvents on log groups under /aws-glue/

sources.title: Using crawlers to populate the Data Catalog
supports: A crawler classifies files to infer format and schema, groups them into tables and partitions by its heuristics, and writes the result to the Data Catalog
A crawler must download a compressed file to process it

sources.title: Preventing a crawler from changing an existing schema
supports: By default a crawler updates the schema in the Data Catalog to match the data source being crawled
Setting the schema change policy's UpdateBehavior to LOG, with partitions inheriting from the table, prevents it

sources.title: Updating the schema, and adding new partitions in the Data Catalog using AWS Glue ETL jobs
supports: A job can register the partitions it writes with enableUpdateCatalog and partitionKeys on a catalog sink, without rerunning a crawler

sources.title: AWS Glue triggers
supports: A trigger starts jobs and crawlers on demand, on a schedule, or on conditions; its states are CREATED, ACTIVATED and DEACTIVATED

sources.title: Time-based schedules for jobs and crawlers
supports: Schedules are cron(Minutes Hours Day-of-month Month Day-of-week Year), in UTC, with a minimum precision of 5 minutes

sources.title: Overview of workflows in AWS Glue
supports: A workflow groups jobs, crawlers and triggers into one graph with a start trigger that is a schedule, on demand, or an EventBridge event

sources.title: AWS Glue Schema registry
supports: The Schema Registry holds versioned schemas (Avro, JSON Schema, Protobuf) for data streams such as Kafka, Amazon MSK and Kinesis Data Streams, with compatibility checks; the page calls it serverless and free to use

sources.title: AWS Glue Data Quality
supports: AWS Glue Data Quality is built on the open-source DeeQu framework and evaluates rules written in DQDL
It has two entry points: tables in the Data Catalog, and AWS Glue ETL jobs; only the ETL entry point identifies the records that failed

sources.title: Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL) reference
supports: A ruleset is a list named Rules in square brackets with comma-separated rules; DQDL is case sensitive
The expression `between x and y` is true in a range that excludes both ends; `in [a, b]` is true for a value in the set

sources.title: ColumnValues
supports: ColumnValues runs an expression against the values of a column; for every expression other than != and NOT IN a NULL row fails the rule

sources.title: IsComplete
supports: IsComplete checks that every value of a column is non-null

sources.title: IsUnique
supports: IsUnique checks that every value of a column is unique

supports: Spark jobs need at least 2 DPUs and are billed per second with a 1-minute minimum on AWS Glue 2.0 and later; Python shell jobs use 0.0625 or 1 DPU with a 1-minute minimum
Crawlers are billed per second with a 10-minute minimum per crawl; the page's example uses 2 DPUs for a crawl
Data quality checks inside an ETL job add to the job's run time and DPU use; they are billed at the job's rate
The first million objects stored in the Data Catalog and the first million requests a month are free
